text: {Name} had moved down a few rows since I came in, as if the show might start again if {he} waited long enough.
{Name} was where I’d left {him}, hat in hand. {He} hadn’t put it on and {he} hadn’t put it down. I’ve seen people stand like that outside a dentist’s.
{Name} had found an aisle seat and was sitting in it the way you sit in a waiting room, ready to be called.
{Name} was reading the programme for the third time, in case the cast had changed.
{Name} hadn’t moved. In a theatre after the show, that’s a kind of statement.
{Name} had a fresh glass in front of {him} and the look of somebody who’d meant to stop at the last one.
{Name} hadn’t moved off {his} stool, and the stool hadn’t complained.
{Name} was turning a glass round on the bar, one slow quarter at a time, like a safe nobody had the numbers to.
{Name} had moved to the end of the bar, where the light was worst. People choose that end for a reason, and it isn’t the light.
{Name} was still there, which at that hour in that room is most of what you can ask of anybody.
{Name} had a cup {he}’d stopped drinking and a newspaper {he}’d stopped reading, and was keeping both for company.
{Name} was at the same table, working through a slice of pie as if it owed {him} money.
{Name} had moved to a table by the wall, where nobody could come up behind {him}.
{Name} hadn’t touched {his} coffee since I came in. It had gone cold out of sheer neglect.
{Name} was buttering a roll {he} didn’t want, slowly, to have something to do with {his} hands.
{Name} had come out onto the landing in {his} slippers, to see what the stairs were saying about {him}.
{Name} was in the kitchen doorway with a dish towel, which in that house was the same as a coat of arms.
{Name} had put the kettle on, not for me, but because the kettle was what {he} did when people came to the door.
{Name} stood in {his} own hall like a visitor, with one hand on the banister.
{Name} had sat down on the bottom stair to wait for me, the way people wait for news they’ve already guessed.
{Name} hadn’t stopped working, which is the one thing a working man can do with a question.
{Name} wiped {his} hands on a rag and kept one eye on whatever {he}’d been doing, in case it got ideas.
{Name} looked up from the work as if I were a mistake in it.
{Name} had kept to the back, where the light didn’t reach and nobody asked.
{Name} was where nobody would look for {him}, except a man who was being paid to.
{Name} hadn’t moved. Some people sit still because they’re comfortable, and some because moving would be noticed.
{Name} watched me come over the way you watch weather.
{Name} saw me coming and found something to do with {his} hands, which didn’t help either of us.
{Name} had been watching me ask the others, and had had time to think about it, which isn’t always an advantage.
{Name} looked up when I came over, and then down, and then up again, the way people check a clock.
{Name} had been waiting to be asked. Most people have. They just don’t say so.
{Name} didn’t get up when I came over, and didn’t ask me to sit, so I did both for {him}.
{Client} watched from the doorway as if I might find {thing} under a cushion and spoil the whole night for both of us.
{Client} stood in the hall with {his} hands in {his} pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed.
{Client} kept out of my way, the way people keep out of the way of a doctor.
{Client} hovered, and then apologised for hovering, and then hovered.
{Client} told me twice where everything usually was. I let {him}. It was {his} flat, and it was the only thing {he} could do.
{Client} sat on the arm of a chair and watched me go over {his} own parlour like a stranger’s.
{Client} stayed by the door. People in a room with a dead man stand where they can leave.
{Client} didn’t come in. I didn’t ask {him} to.
{Client} watched from the landing with {his} coat buttoned to the neck, as if the cold were in the room.
{Client} turned {his} back while I worked, and I was grateful. I don’t like an audience for this part.
I worked slowly. {Client} waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time {he} shifted {his} weight.
I went back over to {name}. {He} saw me coming and had time to wish I wasn’t.
I sat down across from {name} again and opened my notebook at {his} page.
I went back to {name} with my notebook open, which is never good news for anybody.
{Name} hadn’t expected me back so soon. Nobody ever does.
I found {name} where I’d left {him}, and stood close enough that {he} had to look up.
I didn’t sit down this time. Some questions go better standing.
I came back to {name} the way you come back to a sum that won’t add up: slowly, with a pencil.
{Name} saw the notebook in my hand and knew what it meant before I opened my mouth.
